question_html: As per AS 10, when should depreciation begin on an asset?
option_a: From the date the asset is first put to commercial use/production
option_b: From the date the asset is available for use (in the location and condition necessary to operate in the manner intended by management)
option_c: From the beginning of the next financial year after acquisition
option_d: From the date the payment for the asset is made
explanation_html: As per AS 10, depreciation of an asset begins when it is available for use, i.e., when it is in the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by the management. It does NOT begin from the date of actual use or commercial production. For example, if a machine is ready for use on 1st November but the company starts using it on 1st March, depreciation commences from 1st November — not 1st March. The fact that the machine was not used for a period after it was ready is irrelevant. This is a critical and frequently examined principle under AS 10.

question_html: A trader commenced business with ₹12,000 represented by 6,000 units at ₹2 per unit. During the year, he sold all units at ₹3 per unit and withdrew ₹6,000. Price index at beginning = 100; at end = 120. What is the Retained Profit under Financial Capital Maintenance at Current Purchasing Power?
explanation_html:
Step 1: Closing Equity at closing price
Sales = 6,000 × ₹3 = ₹18,000; Drawings = ₹6,000
Closing Equity = ₹18,000 – ₹6,000 = ₹12,000 (represented entirely by cash)

Step 2: Opening Equity restated at closing price (using average price index)
Opening equity at historical cost = ₹12,000
Restated = (₹12,000/100) × 120 = ₹14,400

Step 3: Retained Profit
= Closing Equity – Opening Equity restated
= ₹12,000 – ₹14,400 = (–) ₹2,400 (Loss)

The negative retained profit indicates the trader failed to maintain capital — ₹12,000 is insufficient to buy 6,000 units at new price of ₹2.40 per unit.

question_html: As per AS 29, which of the following statements about reimbursements expected from a third party (e.g., insurance) is correct?
option_a: The net amount (provision minus expected reimbursement) is shown as a single liability in the balance sheet
option_b: The provision is recognised for the full amount of the liability; a separate asset is recognised for the expected reimbursement only when it is virtually certain
option_c: Provision is reduced by the amount of expected reimbursement and only the net provision is recognised
option_d: No provision is needed if insurance covers the full expected loss
explanation_html:
AS 29 prescribes that reimbursements should be treated as follows:

The enterprise must recognise a provision for the full amount of the liability — the fact that a reimbursement is expected does not reduce the obligation itself. A separate asset for the expected reimbursement is recognised on the balance sheet only when it is virtually certain that reimbursement will be received if the enterprise settles the liability.

The maximum amount recognised for the expected reimbursement asset must not exceed the amount of the provision. In the Statement of Profit and Loss, the expense may be presented net of the reimbursement amount. Option (a) is incorrect because both gross liability and gross asset are shown separately (they cannot be netted unless specifically permitted). Option (d) is incorrect — a provision is still required for the full liability.

question_html: Under Present Value convention, an asset generates ₹11,000 after 1 year. The required earning rate is 10% per year. What is the Present Value of this asset?
explanation_html:
Under Present Value convention, assets are carried at the present value of future net cash inflows they are expected to generate.

Formula: P = A × [1/(1+R)ⁿ]
Where A = ₹11,000, R = 10% = 0.10, n = 1 year

P = ₹11,000 × [1/1.10] = ₹11,000 × 0.909 = ₹10,000 (approx.)

This means a receipt of ₹10,000 now is equivalent to receiving ₹11,000 after 1 year at 10% earning rate — because ₹10,000 invested today at 10% grows to ₹11,000 after 1 year.

question_html: Which of the following transactions does NOT result in a cash flow and therefore should not be reported in the Cash Flow Statement?
option_a: Cash received from sale of old machinery
option_b: Issue of bonus shares by capitalisation of reserves
option_c: Redemption of debentures by payment of cash
explanation_html: As per AS 3, investing and financing transactions that do not require the use of cash or cash equivalents should be excluded from the Cash Flow Statement. Issue of bonus shares involves capitalisation of reserves — no cash changes hands. It is therefore a non-cash transaction and should be excluded from the Cash Flow Statement. However, it must be disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements in a way that provides all relevant information. Other options — receipt from machinery sale, debenture redemption, and bank loan repayment — all involve actual cash flows and must be reported in the CFS under investing or financing activities as applicable.

question_html: X Ltd. invested ₹ 600 lakhs in equity shares of Y Ltd. — ₹ 300 lakhs intended as long-term, ₹ 300 lakhs as current. On 31-3-20X1, market value of the entire holding fell to ₹ 200 lakhs (₹ 100 lakhs each) due to Y Ltd. losing a copyright case. The decline is not temporary. What is the total charge to the Statement of Profit and Loss?
option_c: ₹ 200 lakhs for current investments; ₹ 200 lakhs for long-term investments = ₹ 400 lakhs total
option_d: ₹ 200 lakhs (only long-term investment written down since the decline is not temporary)
explanation_html:
Current Investments (₹300 lakhs → ₹100 lakhs): AS 13 requires current investments to be carried at lower of cost and fair value. Since fair value (₹100 lakhs) < cost (₹300 lakhs), write-down = ₹200 lakhs — charged to P&L.

Long-term Investments (₹300 lakhs → ₹100 lakhs): AS 13 states long-term investments are carried at cost, but when there is a decline other than temporary, the carrying amount is reduced to recognise the decline. Losing a copyright case causing significant, permanent value erosion constitutes other-than-temporary decline. Write-down = ₹200 lakhs — charged to P&L.

Total charge = ₹200 + ₹200 = ₹400 lakhs.

question_html: Hindustan Industries sends goods to Cochin Branch at cost plus 25%. Goods received at invoice price = ₹6,00,000. Under the Stock and Debtors Method, what is the loading (profit element) credited to Branch Adjustment Account on goods sent?

Invoice price = Cost × 125%
Loading as a fraction of invoice price = 25/125 = 1/5 = 20%

Loading on ₹6,00,000 (invoice price) = ₹6,00,000 × 1/5 = ₹1,20,000

Journal entry in Branch Adjustment A/c:
Goods Sent to Branch A/c Dr. ₹4,80,000 (cost = 6,00,000 × 100/125)
Branch Adjustment A/c Cr. ₹1,20,000 (loading = 6,00,000 × 25/125)

Actually, the Branch Stock A/c is debited with ₹6,00,000 (invoice price):
Branch Stock A/c Dr. ₹6,00,000 / To Goods Sent to Branch A/c ₹4,80,000 (cost) / To Branch Adjustment A/c ₹1,20,000 (loading)

Per Illustration 6 in the text: 1/5 of ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,20,000 credit to Branch Adjustment A/c.

question_html: XYZ Ltd. proposes to declare 10% dividend out of General Reserves (due to inadequate current year profits). Details: 8,00,000 equity shares × ₹10 = ₹80,00,000; 17,500 9% preference shares × ₹100 = ₹17,50,000; General Reserve = ₹25,00,000; Current year net profit = ₹3,00,000. Average dividend rate (last 3 years) = 12%. What is the amount that can be utilised from General Reserves?
As per Section 123(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, dividend can be declared:
option_a: Out of any reserves including capital reserve
option_b: Only out of current year's profits after providing depreciation
option_c: Out of profits of current financial year or previous undistributed profits, both after providing depreciation, or moneys provided by government; but NOT from reserves other than free reserves
option_d: Out of profits before providing for depreciation
explanation_html:
Section 123(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that no dividend shall be declared or paid except:
(a) Out of profits for that financial year arrived at after providing for depreciation;
(b) Out of profits for any previous financial years arrived at after providing for depreciation and remaining undistributed;
(c) Out of both (a) and (b); or
(d) Out of moneys provided by the Central/State Government for payment of dividend in pursuance of any guarantee.

Critically: No dividend shall be declared from reserves other than FREE reserves. Capital reserves, revaluation reserves, etc. cannot be used for dividend payment. Depreciation must be provided before declaring dividend.

question_html: Which user group of financial statements is primarily interested in information to determine whether their loans and the interest attaching to them will be paid when due?

question_html: As per AS 4 (Revised), theft of cash of ₹ 5 lakhs by the cashier in January 20X1 was detected only in May 20X1. The accounts for the year ended 31st March 20X1 were not yet approved by the Board of Directors. How should this be treated?
option_a: Non-adjusting event — disclose in the Directors' Report only
option_b: Adjusting event — recognise the loss of ₹ 5 lakhs in the accounts for the year ended 31st March 20X1
option_c: Ignore — since the amount was stolen before year-end, no adjustment or disclosure is needed
option_d: Extraordinary item — disclose separately in the Statement of Profit and Loss
explanation_html:
As per AS 4 (Revised), adjustments to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of amounts relating to conditions existing at the balance sheet date.

The theft took place in January 20X1 — i.e., before the balance sheet date of 31st March 20X1. The detection in May 20X1 (after the balance sheet date, but before approval) provides additional evidence of a condition that existed on 31st March 20X1. Therefore, this is an adjusting event and the loss of ₹5 lakhs must be recognised in the accounts for the year ended 31st March 20X1.

question_html: Y Ltd. (transferor) has equity share capital ₹30,00,000 (3,00,000 shares × ₹10). X Ltd. (transferee) issues 3,50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par + 15% preference shares (total PC = ₹53,70,000). Under the Merger (Pooling of Interests) method, what amount is adjusted against reserves, and what is it?
option_a: ₹3,80,000 adjusted against reserves (being net asset excess)
option_b: ₹6,70,000 adjusted as a deduction against X Ltd.'s General Reserve (PC – Y Ltd.'s share capital = ₹53,70,000 – ₹47,00,000)
explanation_html:
Under the Pooling of Interests Method:
Step I: Amount issued by X Ltd. = ₹53,70,000 (PC)
Step II: Share capital of Y Ltd. = ₹47,00,000 (₹30,00,000 equity + ₹17,00,000 preference)
Step III: Difference = ₹53,70,000 – ₹47,00,000 = ₹6,70,000

This ₹6,70,000 is a deduction from X Ltd.'s General Reserve (as the capital issued exceeds the transferor's share capital). Per Illustration 8, this adjustment is debited to General Reserve of X Ltd. (₹500 + adjustment = ₹670 reduction → net ₹(670) in working).

In contrast, under the Purchase Method, this same situation creates a Capital Reserve of ₹3,80,000 (net assets – PC).

question_html: What is the amount to be recognized as Revenue as per AS 9 in the books of Kay Ltd. as on 31 March, 2024?
explanation_html:
Under AS 9 (Revenue Recognition), revenue from sale of goods is recognised when all significant risks and rewards of ownership are transferred.

Mr. Ravi Kumar sale (₹ 22,00,000): This is a bill and hold sale — goods are sold but delivery is postponed at the buyer's request. AS 9 permits revenue recognition when: (i) it is probable the delivery will be made, (ii) the item is on hand and specifically identified, (iii) the buyer acknowledges the deferred delivery instruction. Since the sale is complete and only delivery is postponed at buyer's request, revenue of ₹ 22,00,000 is recognised.

Sheetal Enterprises — approval basis (₹ 2,00,000): Approval period is 3 months from Jan 1, 2024, expiring on March 31, 2024. Till March 31: disapproval for 25% (₹ 50,000 not recognised), approval for 50% (₹ 1,00,000 recognised). Remaining 25% — approval period expires on March 31, so it is deemed sold: ₹ 50,000 recognised. Total recognised = ₹ 1,00,000 + ₹ 50,000 = ₹ 1,50,000.

Total Revenue = ₹ 22,00,000 + ₹ 1,50,000 = ₹ 23,50,000.

question_html: How should the dividend paid by the Company should be disclosed in the Cash Flows Statement:
explanation_html:
As per AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements), dividends paid by a company are classified as cash flows from Financing Activities.

Financing activities are those that result in changes in the size and composition of the owner's capital and borrowings of the enterprise. Since dividends are paid to shareholders (providers of finance), the payment is a financing activity.

Note: Dividends received (by the company on its investments) may be classified as Operating or Investing activities. But dividends paid are always Financing. AS 3 specifically states dividends paid should be classified as financing cash flows.

question_html: Saras Ltd. accrued GST liability of ₹ 5,00,000 for March 20X2, debiting it to P&L, payable by 21st April 20X2. As per Section 43B of the Income Tax Act, this is deductible for tax only on payment basis (i.e., in FY 20X2-X3). Tax rate = 30%. What is the deferred tax impact as at 31st March 20X2?
option_b: Deferred Tax Asset of ₹ 1,50,000 — since the tax deduction will be available in the future
option_c: No deferred tax — GST is a permanent difference
explanation_html:
This is a classic timing difference under Section 43B:

In P&L (accounting): GST of ₹5,00,000 is expensed in FY 20X1-X2 (March 20X2) on accrual basis.
For Tax: Under Section 43B, this expense is deductible ONLY when actually paid — i.e., in FY 20X2-X3 (paid by 21st April 20X2).

Therefore, accounting income is lower than taxable income in FY 20X1-X2 (tax doesn't yet recognise this deduction). This means the company pays more tax currently but will get a deduction in the future when the expense is paid. This creates a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) = ₹5,00,000 × 30% = ₹1,50,000 representing the future tax benefit. In FY 20X2-X3, when the GST is paid and deducted for tax, the DTA of ₹1,50,000 reverses.

question_html: Under AS 9, when an uncertainty arises about the collectability of an amount already recognised as revenue in the Statement of Profit and Loss, the uncollectable amount should be:
option_a: Deducted from (adjusted against) the previously recognised revenue
option_b: Recognised as an expense (bad debt) rather than as an adjustment to revenue
explanation_html:
AS 9 (and also AS 7 for construction contracts) makes a clear distinction: when an uncertainty arises about collectability of an amount already included in revenue and recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss, the uncollectable amount (or the amount for which recovery has ceased to be probable) should be recognised as an expense (bad debt) — NOT as an adjustment to/deduction from revenue.

This is an important principle: once revenue is correctly recognised, it remains in revenue. The subsequent doubtful collectability creates a separate bad debt expense. This maintains the integrity of the revenue figure and separately shows the credit risk outcome. This contrasts with situations where collectability was uncertain at the time of performance — in those cases, revenue recognition is postponed.

question_html: What is the total cost that should be capitalized for a trademark related to the new process?
explanation_html:
Under AS 26 (Intangible Assets), an intangible asset is recognised at cost. The cost of a separately acquired intangible asset includes its purchase price and any directly attributable costs of preparing the asset for its intended use.

Costs incurred by AB Ltd.:

  • Trademark acquisition cost: ₹70,00,000 → Capitalise (direct purchase cost).
  • Employee benefits for testing the new process: ₹3,00,000 → Capitalise (directly attributable cost of preparing the asset for use).
  • Product promotion costs: ₹2,00,000 → Expense (advertising/promotion costs cannot be capitalised as per AS 26 — they do not create an identifiable asset).

Total cost to capitalise = ₹70,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 = ₹73,00,000.

question_html: Jammu branch of Best New Delhi receives goods at invoice price (cost + 20%) and sells at cost + 50%. Opening stock = ₹2,20,000 (invoice). Goods received = ₹11,00,000 (invoice). Sales = ₹12,00,000. What is the closing stock at invoice price?
explanation_html:
Calculating closing stock at invoice price:

Price relationships: Cost = 100; Invoice = 120; Sale = 150

Cost of goods sold (at cost): Sales × (100/150) = ₹12,00,000 × 100/150 = ₹8,00,000
Cost of goods sold (at invoice price): ₹8,00,000 × 120/100 = ₹9,60,000

Closing stock at invoice price:
= Opening stock + Goods received – Cost of goods sold (at invoice)
= ₹2,20,000 + ₹11,00,000 – ₹9,60,000
= ₹3,60,000

Stock Reserve = ₹3,60,000 × 20/120 = ₹60,000 (unrealised profit in closing stock)

Per Illustration 5, the same result is shown in the Branch Trading Account.

question_html: In inter-branch transactions, Kolkata Branch incurred ₹1,000 on advertisement on behalf of Delhi Branch. All inter-branch transactions are routed through Head Office. What is the entry in Delhi Branch books?

In Kolkata Books: Head Office A/c Dr. ₹1,000 / To Cash A/c Cr. ₹1,000 (paid on behalf of Delhi, HO to reimburse)

In Delhi Books: Advertisement A/c Dr. ₹1,000 / To Head Office A/c Cr. ₹1,000 (expense incurred on behalf of Delhi, payable to HO)

question_html: Sahil Ltd agreed to sell its factory located in Assam to Kali Ltd on 4.12.2023. It entered into a sale deed (transferring all significant risks and rewards of ownership) on 1.2.2024. But the transaction was registered with the registrar on 30.5.2024. When should the sale and gain be recognized?

option_b: Both sale and gain should be recognized on 30.5.2024.
option_c: The sale should be recognized as on balance sheet date but gain should be recognized on 30.5.2024.
option_d: Both sale and gain should be recognized on 4.12.2023.
explanation_html:
As per AS 9 (Revenue Recognition), revenue is recognised when all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred.

The sale deed transferring risks and rewards was signed on 1 February 2024 — before the balance sheet date of 31 March 2024. Registration (30.5.2024) is a legal formality and does not determine the accounting recognition point.

Since both the sale and gain arose before 31.3.2024, both are recognised in the year ending 31 March 2024.

question_html: Under the Revaluation Model (AS 10), a plot of land (carrying amount ₹ 1,00,000) is first revalued downward to ₹ 90,000 at end of Year 2 (decrease ₹ 10,000). At end of Year 4, due to increase in market values, fair value rises to ₹ 1,05,000 (increase ₹ 15,000). What is the correct accounting treatment for the upward revaluation in Year 4?
explanation_html:
The revaluation sequence is:
Year 2: Downward revaluation of ₹10,000 → Since no previous Revaluation Reserve exists, the full ₹10,000 is charged to P&L (Statement of Profit and Loss).

Year 4: Upward revaluation of ₹15,000. AS 10 states: when an asset is subsequently increased (after an initial decrease), the increase is recognised in the Statement of P&L to the extent it reverses a revaluation decrease previously recognised in P&L. The balance, if any, is credited to Revaluation Reserve.

₹10,000 → Credited to P&L (reversal of the earlier P&L charge)
₹5,000 → Credited to Revaluation Reserve (excess above reversal)

Option (c) is correct.

question_html: As per AS 1, which of the following statements about disclosure of changes in accounting policies is incorrect?
option_a: Any change in an accounting policy which has a material effect should be disclosed
option_b: The amount by which any item is affected by the change should be disclosed to the extent ascertainable; if not ascertainable, the fact should be indicated
option_c: If a change has no material effect in the current period but is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods, the fact of such change should be disclosed in the current period
option_d: If a change has a material effect in the current period and is expected to have a material effect in later periods, it need only be disclosed in later periods
explanation_html: Option (d) is incorrect because: if a change has a material effect in the current period, it must be disclosed in the current period itself, not deferred to later periods. As per AS 1: (i) Any material change must be disclosed. (ii) The amount of effect must be disclosed to the extent ascertainable; if not ascertainable, the fact should be indicated. (iii) A change expected to have material effect in later periods must be disclosed in the current period when the change is adopted, even if it has no material effect currently. All three options (a), (b), (c) are correct statements under AS 1.

question_html: What is the amount of impairment loss on 31.3.2024?
explanation_html:
Under AS 28 (Impairment of Assets), impairment loss = Carrying amount − Recoverable amount. Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use.

Step 1 — Carrying value before revaluation (31.3.2022):

Cost = ₹25 lakhs. Life = 8 years from 1.4.2018. By 31.3.2022 = 4 years elapsed.

Annual depreciation = ₹25/8 = ₹3.125 lakhs. Accumulated depreciation (4 yrs) = ₹12.5 lakhs. Carrying value at 31.3.2022 (pre-revaluation) = ₹25 − ₹12.5 = ₹12.5 lakhs.

Step 2 — Revaluation on 31.3.2022:

Revalued to ₹18 lakhs. Revaluation surplus = ₹18 − ₹12.5 = ₹5.5 lakhs → credited to Revaluation Reserve.

Revised useful life = 5 years from 31.3.2022. New annual depreciation = ₹18/5 = ₹3.6 lakhs.

Old annual depreciation = ₹3.125 lakhs. Increased depreciation = ₹0.475 lakhs per year → written off against Revaluation Reserve each year.

Step 3 — Carrying value on 31.3.2024 (2 years after revaluation):

Carrying value = ₹18 − (₹3.6 × 2) = ₹18 − ₹7.2 = ₹10.8 lakhs.

Step 4 — Impairment on 31.3.2024:

Recoverable amount = ₹6 lakhs. Impairment loss = ₹10.8 − ₹6 = ₹4.8 lakhs.

question_html: As per AS 21, which of the following correctly defines Minority Interest?
option_a: The total share capital of the subsidiary held by outsiders
option_b: That part of the net results of operations and of the net assets of a subsidiary attributable to interests which are not owned, directly or indirectly through subsidiaries, by the parent
option_c: The portion of goodwill attributable to minority shareholders
option_d: The preference share capital of the subsidiary not held by the holding company
explanation_html:
AS 21 defines Minority Interest as "that part of the net results of operations and of the net assets of a subsidiary attributable to interests which are not owned, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), by the parent."

Minority Interest consists of:
(i) The amount of equity attributable to minorities at the date on which investment in a subsidiary is made; and
(ii) The minorities' share of movements in equity since the date the parent-subsidiary relationship came in existence.

As per Schedule III, minority interests in the balance sheet within equity shall be presented separately from the equity of the owners of the parent. Minority interest in income shall also be separately presented in the consolidated income statement.

question_html: The concept of GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) is a combination of:
option_a: International Financial Reporting Standards and local taxation laws
option_b: Authoritative standards set by policy boards and commonly accepted ways of recording and reporting accounting information
option_c: Standards issued by IASB only, applicable uniformly across all countries
option_d: Government regulations and court judgements on accounting matters
explanation_html:
As defined in the ICAI study material, GAAP is a combination of:
1. Authoritative standards (set by policy boards such as ASB, IASB etc.)
2. The commonly accepted ways of recording and reporting accounting information
At the international level, such authoritative standards are known as IFRS; in India, they are known as Accounting Standards (ASs) and Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS). GAAP is not limited to taxation laws or court judgements.

question_html: What is the maximum number of shares to be bought back as per debt-equity ratio?
explanation_html:
Under Section 68 of the Companies Act 2013, post buy-back, the debt-to-equity ratio must not exceed 2:1.

Existing loan funds = ₹52,00,000. Post buy-back debt must be ≤ 2 × post buy-back equity.

Free reserves for buy-back (excluding Revaluation Reserve and Infrastructure Development Reserve, which is a statutory reserve under Income Tax Act and cannot be used):

General Reserve: ₹20,50,000 + Securities Premium: ₹7,50,000 + P&L: ₹2,00,000 = ₹30,00,000.

Let x = number of shares bought back at ₹25 each.

Post buy-back equity = Equity share capital − (x × ₹10) + Reserves remaining.

Post buy-back equity fund = ₹24,00,000 + ₹51,70,000 − (x × ₹25) = ₹75,70,000 − 25x.

Condition: ₹52,00,000 ≤ 2 × (₹75,70,000 − 25x)

₹52,00,000 ≤ ₹1,51,40,000 − 50x → 50x ≤ ₹99,40,000 → x ≤ 1,98,800 shares.

But also: buy-back cannot exceed 25% of paid-up equity capital = 25% × 2,40,000 shares = 60,000 shares.

And resources available = ₹30,00,000 ÷ ₹25 = 1,20,000 shares maximum.

The binding constraint from the debt-equity test combined with the 25% cap: maximum permissible by debt-equity = 80,000 shares (at which point equity = ₹75,70,000 − ₹20,00,000 = ₹55,70,000; debt/equity = ₹52,00,000/₹55,70,000 < 2). The question asks specifically for the debt-equity test result = 80,000 shares.

question_html: In the internal reconstruction of ABC Ltd., 9% Debenture holders accept plant and machinery in full settlement of their ₹12,00,000 dues. The plant and machinery has a book value of ₹9,00,000. What entry is passed?
option_a: 9% Debentures Dr. ₹12,00,000 / To Plant & Machinery Cr. ₹12,00,000
option_b: 9% Debentures Dr. ₹12,00,000 / To Plant & Machinery Cr. ₹9,00,000 / To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹3,00,000
option_d: Capital Reduction Dr. ₹3,00,000 / To Plant & Machinery Cr. ₹3,00,000
explanation_html:
The debenture holders accept plant and machinery at full settlement of ₹12,00,000, but the book value of the plant is only ₹9,00,000. There is a gain on this settlement:

Debenture liability = ₹12,00,000 (extinguished)
Book value of plant = ₹9,00,000 (transferred)
Gain = ₹3,00,000 → Credited to Capital Reduction A/c

Journal entry per Illustration 6 (ABC Ltd.):
9% Debentures A/c Dr. ₹12,00,000
   To Plant & Machinery A/c Cr. ₹9,00,000
   To Capital Reduction A/c Cr. ₹3,00,000

The Capital Reduction A/c is credited because the debenture holders effectively surrendered ₹3,00,000 (they accepted an asset worth ₹9,00,000 in lieu of ₹12,00,000 dues).

question_html: P Ltd. acquired 1,05,000 shares (70%) of Q Ltd. for ₹ 12,00,000. Q Ltd.'s capital = ₹ 15,00,000 (1,50,000 shares × ₹10), Pre-incorporation profits = ₹ 30,000, P&L = ₹ 60,000 at acquisition date. Later, Q Ltd. issues bonus shares (1:2 ratio) from post-acquisition General Reserve. How does the bonus issue affect the Cost of Control/Capital Reserve?
option_a: Goodwill reduces by the amount of bonus shares
option_b: Capital Reserve increases due to bonus shares
option_c: The bonus shares are taken into account by increasing the face value component in the cost of control computation; Capital Reserve increases
option_d: No effect on cost of control — bonus shares don't change net worth
explanation_html:
From Illustration 9 of the ICAI text:

Before bonus issue: P Ltd. holds 1,05,000 shares (70%); Cost = ₹12,00,000; Pre-acquisition equity = SC ₹10,50,000 + capital profits ₹63,000 (70% × ₹90,000) = ₹11,13,000; Goodwill = ₹87,000.

After bonus issue (1:2): Q Ltd. issues bonus shares from post-acquisition General Reserve. P Ltd. gets 52,500 bonus shares. P Ltd.'s total shares = 1,57,500 (70% of 2,25,000 new total).

Now face value of P Ltd.'s investment = SC ₹15,75,000 (70% of ₹22,50,000). Pre-acquisition equity = ₹15,75,000 + ₹63,000 = ₹16,38,000. Cost = ₹12,00,000. Capital Reserve = ₹4,38,000.

The bonus shares (from post-acquisition reserves) create a Capital Reserve by increasing the face value attributable to P Ltd. beyond the original investment cost.

question_html: M Ltd. decides to buy back 20% of its equity capital (3,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each) at ₹15 per share. It also sold investments (cost ₹30 lakhs) for ₹25 lakhs. What is the premium payable on buy-back and from which source should it be adjusted?

Face value = ₹10 per share

Total premium = 60,000 × ₹5 = ₹3,00,000

In M Ltd.'s case, from Illustration 1: Securities Premium A/c (₹3 lakhs) Dr. → To Premium Payable on Buy-Back A/c ₹3 lakhs. The Securities Premium balance was ₹5 lakhs (₹500 in ₹000s), sufficient to absorb the ₹3 lakhs premium.

question_html: Under AS 9, which of the following correctly states when revenue from sale of goods should be recognised?
option_a: When cash is received from the buyer
option_b: When the invoice is raised by the seller
option_c: When the seller has transferred property in goods or all significant risks and rewards of ownership to the buyer, retains no effective control, and there is no significant uncertainty about the consideration
option_d: When the goods are physically delivered to the buyer's premises
explanation_html:
AS 9 prescribes that revenue from sale of goods should be recognised when all three conditions are met:
(i) The seller has transferred to the buyer the property in goods for a price, OR all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the buyer and the seller retains no effective control; and
(ii) No significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration.

Cash receipt is NOT required — revenue can be recognised even for credit sales. Physical delivery does not always determine the transfer of risks/rewards (e.g., goods in transit, goods held for customer). Invoice date is not determinative. The key is economic transfer of risks and rewards, not legal formalities.

question_html: Income earned is always associated with:
option_a: Either increase of asset or increase of liability
option_b: Either increase of asset or reduction of liability
option_c: Either reduction of asset or reduction of liability

explanation_html:

- Discount earned on settlement of creditor → Decrease in liability
This is why a bank does not recognise interest earned on non-performing assets — the corresponding asset (advances) cannot be recognised.

question_html: Under Method II (grant treated as deferred income), Z Ltd. received a grant of ₹ 10 lakhs for an asset costing ₹ 50 lakhs (5 years, SLM, salvage ₹ 5 lakhs). How much grant income is recognised in the P&L each year?
explanation_html:
Under Method II, grants related to depreciable assets are treated as deferred income which is recognised in P&L on a systematic and rational basis over the useful life of the asset. The most common approach is to recognise the deferred grant proportionately to the depreciation charged.

Annual depreciation = (₹50 – ₹5) ÷ 5 = ₹9 lakhs. The deferred grant income is recognised at ₹10 ÷ 5 = ₹2 lakhs per year (proportionate to life). Net effect on P&L: Depreciation expense = ₹9 lakhs; Grant income = ₹2 lakhs; Net charge = ₹7 lakhs — same as Method I's net effect, demonstrating that both methods produce the same P&L outcome over time.

question_html: A Ltd. (75% holding) purchases goods costing ₹ 150 lakhs from B Ltd. (subsidiary) at ₹ 200 lakhs. All goods remain unsold with A Ltd. at year-end. This is an upstream transaction. How much is eliminated from minority interest?
option_a: Nil — only consolidated profits are reduced by ₹ 50 lakhs
option_b: ₹ 37.50 lakhs from consolidated profits; ₹ 12.50 lakhs from minority interest
option_d: ₹ 25 lakhs each from consolidated profits and minority interest
explanation_html:
This is an upstream transaction (subsidiary B Ltd. sells to holding company A Ltd.). The profit of ₹50 lakhs is earned by B Ltd. (subsidiary), which is shared between A Ltd. (75%) and minority (25%).

Since goods remain unsold with A Ltd., the ₹50 lakhs unrealised profit must be eliminated:

1. Eliminate intra-group sale ₹200 lakhs and purchase ₹200 lakhs.
2. Reduce closing inventory by ₹50 lakhs.
3. Eliminate from:
  • A Ltd.'s (majority's) share of profits: 75% × ₹50 = ₹37.50 lakhs
  • Minority interest: 25% × ₹50 = ₹12.50 lakhs

The key difference from downstream: in upstream, the profit is in the subsidiary's books and belongs to BOTH majority and minority — so the elimination affects both.

question_html: A Ltd. takes over B Ltd. and discharges consideration as: 42,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par; 15% preference shares of ₹100 each to discharge ₹1,70,000 preference share capital at 10% premium; debentures of B Ltd. (₹50,000) converted into equal debentures of A Ltd. What is the Purchase Consideration under AS 14?
option_c: ₹ 5,90,000 (only equity and preference shares at par)
explanation_html:
AS 14 defines consideration as the aggregate of shares and securities issued AND payments made to shareholders of the transferor company.

Equity shares: 42,000 × ₹10 = ₹4,20,000 ✓
15% Preference shares: ₹1,70,000 + 10% premium (₹17,000) = ₹1,87,000 ✓
Total Purchase Consideration = ₹4,20,000 + ₹1,87,000 = ₹6,07,000

Debentures (₹50,000): NOT included — the payment to debenture holders is NOT covered by the term 'consideration' under AS 14. Consideration relates only to payments to shareholders (equity and preference shareholders) of the transferor company. Debenture conversion is treated separately as assumption of liabilities.

question_html: Which of the following statements about Timeliness as a constraint on relevant and reliable information is CORRECT?
option_a: Timely information is always more reliable than late information
option_b: If reporting is delayed until all aspects are known, the information may be highly reliable but may be of little use to users who had to make decisions in the interim
option_c: Timeliness always takes precedence over reliability in achieving quality financial reporting
option_d: Providing early information always impairs both relevance and reliability equally
explanation_html:
As per the Framework on Timeliness as a constraint:
- Early reporting (before all aspects are known) = timely but may impair reliability
- Delayed reporting (after all aspects are known) = highly reliable but may lose relevance for users who had to make decisions earlier
Thus, if reporting is delayed until all aspects are known, the information may be highly reliable but of little use to users who had to make decisions in the interim. The overriding consideration is how best to satisfy the information needs of users — management must balance timeliness and reliability.

question_html: As per AS 11, goods were purchased on 1st January 20X1 for US$ 15,000 at ₹ 75 per USD. Exchange rate on 31st March 20X1 = ₹ 74. Payment made on 7th July 20X1 at ₹ 73. What are the exchange gains/losses recognised in FY 20X1 and FY 20X2 respectively?
explanation_html:
As per AS 11:

Initial recording (1st Jan 20X1): Creditors = US$15,000 × ₹75 = ₹11,25,000.

Balance sheet date (31st March 20X1): Creditors restated at closing rate = ₹74: ₹11,10,000. Exchange gain = ₹15,000 (creditor decreased from ₹11,25,000 to ₹11,10,000) → Credited to P&L for FY 20X1.

Settlement (7th July 20X1): Creditors paid at ₹73: ₹10,95,000. Exchange gain = ₹15,000 (creditor decreased from ₹11,10,000 to ₹10,95,000) → Credited to P&L for FY 20X2.

question_html: What is the carrying amount of investment as on 31st March, 2024 as per AS 13 and suggest the treatment of dividend received from P. Ltd.?
option_a: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ₹ 72,000 and the dividend is deducted from the nominal value of investment.
option_b: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ₹90,000 and the dividend is credited to Profit & Loss A/c.
option_c: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ₹ 1,00,000 and the dividend is credited to Profit & Loss A/c.
option_d: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is 82,000 and the dividend is deducted from the cost of investment.
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), for current investments in equity shares, dividend received is treated as income (credited to P&L) unless the dividend is declared out of pre-acquisition profits, in which case it is deducted from the cost of investment.

Mr. Vikram purchased shares on 25th March, 2024. P. Ltd. declared and paid dividend on 30th March, 2024 for the year 2023-24. Since Mr. Vikram purchased the shares on 25th March 2024, the dividend for the entire year 2023-24 relates to pre-acquisition profits (profits earned before he became a shareholder).

Dividend received = 9,000 shares × ₹ 10 FV × 20% = ₹ 18,000

Carrying amount = Cost − Pre-acquisition dividend = ₹ 1,00,000 − ₹ 18,000 = ₹ 82,000

The dividend is deducted from the cost of investment, not credited to P&L, because it represents recovery of pre-acquisition earnings included in the purchase price.

question_html: Under AS 7, which of the following is NOT a valid method for determining the stage of completion of a construction contract?
option_a: The proportion that contract costs incurred bear to the estimated total contract costs
option_c: Completion of a physical proportion of the contract work
option_d: Progress payments and advances received from customers
explanation_html:
AS 7 specifically states that the stage of completion may be determined by:
(a) Proportion of costs incurred to estimated total contract costs;
(b) Surveys of work performed;
(c) Completion of a physical proportion of the contract work.

AS 7 also explicitly states that progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the work performed — they are NOT a reliable basis for determining stage of completion. A contractor may receive large advance payments before significant work is done, or receive payments later even after substantial work. Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.

question_html: M/s KJ sells goods at invoice value of ₹ 5 lakhs to M/s TH on 1st January 20X1, with a commitment to repurchase the same goods back from M/s TH on 31st March at ₹ 6 lakhs. Under AS 9, how should this transaction be recorded by M/s KJ?
option_a: Record revenue of ₹ 5 lakhs on 1st January 20X1; record purchase of ₹ 6 lakhs on 31st March 20X1
option_b: Record revenue of ₹ 5 lakhs less the repurchase obligation of ₹ 6 lakhs — net loss of ₹ 1 lakh
option_c: Record as a borrowing (financing arrangement) — Bank Dr., Loan from M/s TH Cr. ₹ 5 lakhs; no revenue recognised
option_d: Defer revenue recognition until 31st March 20X1 when the repurchase commitment expires
explanation_html:
AS 9 specifically addresses sale and repurchase arrangements. When a seller sells goods but has an obligation or option to repurchase those goods, this is considered a financing arrangement, NOT a sale. The risks and rewards of ownership have not genuinely been transferred — the seller retains effective control through the repurchase obligation.

Therefore, in M/s KJ's books:
1st January 20X1: Bank A/c Dr. ₹5 lakhs; Loan from M/s TH Cr. ₹5 lakhs (borrowing, not sale).
No revenue is recognised.
The difference of ₹1 lakh between repurchase price and sale price represents interest on the borrowing.

question_html: Accounting Standards issued by the Accounting Standards Board of ICAI establish standards that have to be complied with by business entities so that the financial statements are prepared in accordance with GAAP. However, which of the following statements about the legal enforceability of ICAI's Accounting Standards is TRUE?
option_a: ICAI, being a legislative body, can enforce compliance with its standards on all enterprises in India
option_b: ICAI, not being a legislative body, can enforce compliance with its standards only on its members
option_c: Accounting Standards issued by ICAI can override laws and local regulations
option_d: ICAI standards are enforced by the Ministry of Finance on all public sector enterprises
explanation_html: As per the study material on Status of Accounting Standards: The Institute (ICAI), not being a legislative body, can enforce compliance with its standards only on its members. Also, the standards cannot override laws and local regulations. In case of any conflict, Statute would prevail over Accounting Standards. However, ASs are made mandatory from the dates specified in respective standards and are generally applicable to all enterprises, subject to certain exceptions.

question_html: X Ltd. commenced a construction contract on 01-04-20X1. Fixed contract price = ₹ 2,00,000. Cost incurred in 20X1-X2 = ₹ 81,000 for 45% work. Cost incurred in 20X2-X3 = ₹ 89,000 for remaining 55%. What is the contract revenue to be recognised in 20X2-X3?
explanation_html:
Under the percentage of completion method:

20X1-X2 (45% work): Revenue = 45% × ₹2,00,000 = ₹90,000; Cost = ₹81,000; Profit = ₹9,000.

20X2-X3 (55% work): Revenue = 55% × ₹2,00,000 = ₹1,10,000; Cost = ₹89,000; Profit = ₹21,000.

Total contract revenue recognised over both years = ₹90,000 + ₹1,10,000 = ₹2,00,000 = Full contract price. Each year's revenue is based on the proportion of work completed in that year, multiplied by the fixed contract price.

question_html: Which of the following statements about buy-back of shares is CORRECT as per the Companies Act, 2013?
option_a: Partly paid shares can be bought back if the company has sufficient free reserves
option_b: A company can buy-back shares through its subsidiary company if approved by the Board
option_c: Only fully paid-up shares can be bought back
option_d: Revaluation reserve can be used for buy-back since it is part of Reserves and Surplus
explanation_html:
The Companies Act, 2013 prescribes several conditions for buy-back, including:

Section 68(2)(f): All the shares or other specified securities for buy-back must be fully paid-up. Partly paid shares CANNOT be bought back under any circumstances.

Section 70 prohibits buy-back through subsidiary companies — so option (b) is incorrect.

Revaluation reserve represents unrealised profits/gains and cannot be used for buy-back — it is specifically excluded from free reserves for this purpose (option d is incorrect).

The correct statement is option (c): Only fully paid-up shares are eligible for buy-back.

question_html: A Ltd. (holding company, 80% stake) sells goods costing ₹ 180 lakhs to B Ltd. (subsidiary) at ₹ 200 lakhs. All goods remain unsold with B Ltd. at year-end. This is a downstream transaction. What consolidation adjustment is required?
option_a: Reduce consolidated profits by ₹ 16 lakhs (80% of ₹ 20 lakhs) and inventory by ₹ 20 lakhs; minority interest unaffected
option_b: Reduce consolidated profits by ₹ 20 lakhs (full unrealised profit) and inventory by ₹ 20 lakhs; minority interest unaffected
option_c: Reduce consolidated profits by ₹ 16 lakhs and minority interest by ₹ 4 lakhs; reduce inventory by ₹ 20 lakhs
option_d: No adjustment needed as the goods haven't left the group
explanation_html:
This is a downstream transaction (holding company sells to subsidiary). The profit (₹20 lakhs) is earned by the holding company.

Since the goods remain unsold with B Ltd. (subsidiary), the ₹20 lakhs profit is unrealised from the group's perspective.

Adjustment required:
1. Eliminate intra-group sale ₹200 lakhs (from consolidated revenue) and intra-group purchase ₹200 lakhs (from consolidated cost).
2. Reduce consolidated profits (holding company's P&L) by full ₹20 lakhs.
3. Reduce closing inventory by ₹20 lakhs (to cost to group = ₹180 lakhs).

Minority interest is unaffected — the profit was entirely in the holding company. This contrasts with upstream transactions where the minority interest also shares in the elimination.

question_html: X Ltd. received a grant of ₹ 20 crore for a machine costing ₹ 80 crore. X Ltd. follows the policy of deducting the grant from asset cost. Useful life = 10 years; no salvage value; SLM depreciation. What is the annual depreciation expense in P&L?
explanation_html:
Under Method I (grant deducted from asset cost):
Net asset cost = ₹80 crore – ₹20 crore (grant) = ₹60 crore.
No salvage value; Useful life = 10 years.
Annual depreciation = ₹60 crore ÷ 10 = ₹6 crore per year.

Option (a) ₹10 crore = wrong; that would be depreciation on ₹80 crore without deducting the grant. Option (d) ₹8 crore = wrong; that would be depreciation on ₹80 crore at a different rate. The grant has correctly reduced the depreciable base from ₹80 crore to ₹60 crore.

question_html: As per the Framework, the definition of an Asset is:
option_a: A resource owned by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise
option_b: A resource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise
option_c: A resource owned and controlled by the enterprise from which present economic benefits flow to the enterprise
option_d: Any tangible item held by the enterprise for use in production or supply of goods and services
explanation_html:
As per the Framework, an asset is defined as: 'A resource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise.'
Key points: The word is 'controlled' (not 'owned') — so an asset need not be legally owned. For example, a lessee recognises an asset taken on finance lease even though ownership lies with the lessor. Also, the benefits must be future economic benefits. The resource need not have physical substance (e.g., patents, copyrights are assets).

question_html: Exe Ltd. (70% holding) acquired shares of Zed Ltd. at ₹ 20 per share. Zed declared dividend @ 20% on face value ₹ 10 per share on the date of acquisition. This dividend was paid out of pre-acquisition profits. How does this affect the Goodwill computation?
option_a: Dividend is treated as revenue income and credited to P&L; does not affect goodwill
option_b: Dividend (pre-acquisition) is deducted from the cost of investment before computing goodwill/capital reserve
option_c: Dividend is added to the net assets of Zed Ltd. before computing goodwill
option_d: Dividend has no effect since it is declared on the date of acquisition
explanation_html:
When a dividend is declared from pre-acquisition profits, it represents a return of part of the investment cost rather than income. AS 13 states that such dividends should be deducted from the cost of investment before computing goodwill.

In Illustration 3 (Exe Ltd./Zed Ltd.): Number of shares purchased = ₹70 lakhs ÷ ₹20 = 3.5 lakh shares. Dividend = 20% × ₹10 × 3.5 lakh = ₹7 lakhs. This ₹7 lakhs is deducted from cost (₹70 – ₹7 = ₹63 lakhs) to arrive at effective cost for goodwill computation. This results in Capital Reserve of ₹33.95 lakhs (as shown in the ICAI illustration).

question_html: H Ltd. acquired 8,000 shares of S Ltd. (1st July 20X1). S Ltd.'s Profit & Loss on 1st April 20X1 = ₹ 30,000; profit for the year = ₹ 40,000 (accruing evenly). What is the pre-acquisition profit from H Ltd.'s perspective for the 80% stake?
explanation_html:
H Ltd. acquired shares on 1st July 20X1 (mid-year). Profits must be time-apportioned.

Pre-acquisition period = April to June 20X1 = 3 months (out of 12).
Pre-acquisition profit of S Ltd. = Opening balance ₹30,000 + profit earned up to 1st July = ₹30,000 + (3/12 × ₹40,000) = ₹30,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹40,000 total (of S Ltd.)

Wait — Per H Ltd. (acquisition on 1st July, 80% = 8,000/10,000):
Pre-acquisition profits of S = ₹30,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹40,000
H Ltd.'s pre-acquisition share = 80% × ₹40,000 = ₹32,000

But per Illustration 11 in the text, pre-acquisition = 80% × [30,000 + 3/12(40,000-30,000)] = 80% × ₹32,500 = ₹26,000, using only the change in P&L during the year. The interpretation depends on whether full opening balance or only the year's profit is time-split. Per ICAI illustration 11: pre-acquisition = 80% × (30,000 + 3/12 × 10,000) = ₹26,000.

question_html: The Framework recognises four alternative measurement bases for elements of financial statements. Which of the following is NOT one of the four?
explanation_html:
The Framework recognises the following four alternative measurement bases:
1. Historical Cost – acquisition price
2. Current Cost – amount payable if the same/equivalent asset was acquired currently
3. Realisable (Settlement) Value – amount currently realisable on sale
4. Present Value – present value of future net cash flows
Replacement Cost is not separately recognised as a measurement basis in the Framework. It is sometimes confused with current cost, but they are not identical concepts in strict accounting terminology.

question_html: Cost of current investment acquired was ₹ 1000 but the fair value was ₹ 800. The Investment was recorded at ₹ 800. Now the fair value of Investment is Rs 1200. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_a: No change is required and it will continue at ₹ 800
option_b: Current investment will be recorded at ₹ 1000 and gain of ₹ 200 will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_c: Current investment will be recorded at ₹ 1200 and gain of ₹ 400 will be credited to profit and loss account.
option_d: Current investment will be recorded at ₹ 1200 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.
explanation_html:
Under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments), current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value.

When the investment was first recorded: Cost = ₹1,000, Fair value = ₹800. Lower of cost/fair value = ₹800 → recorded at ₹800. A loss of ₹200 was recognised in P&L at that time.

Now fair value has risen to ₹1,200.

Under AS 13, the carrying amount of current investments can be increased up to cost (i.e., reversal of previous write-down) when fair value recovers. Any increase above cost cannot be recognised as income (to avoid gain beyond original cost).

Maximum carrying value = Cost = ₹1,000. The investment is written back up to cost → gain recognised in P&L = ₹1,000 − ₹800 = ₹200.

The investment cannot be carried at ₹1,200 (above cost) — that is not permitted under AS 13 for current investments. Therefore: record at ₹1,000 and credit gain of ₹200 to P&L.

question_html: Amar made an application, his wife Abhilasha being other proposed subscriber and got reserved a name for incorporation of a private limited company but the Registrar of Companies, Delhi and Haryana, much before the incorporation, found that the name was applied by furnishing wrong information.
option_a: The reserved name shall be cancelled by the ROC because the name was applied by furnishing wrong information and Amar who made the application shall be liable to a penalty up to Rs. One lac.

question_html: EXOX Ltd. received a sales tax demand of ₹ 2.76 crore which it paid under protest. The company is appealing against additions of ₹ 2.10 crore but NOT appealing against the remaining ₹ 0.66 crore. How should these amounts be treated in the financial statements under AS 29?
option_b: Provide for ₹ 2.10 crore (full appeal amount); disclose ₹ 0.66 crore as contingent liability
option_c: Provide for ₹ 0.66 crore (not appealed = accepted liability); show ₹ 2.76 crore under Loans & Advances; disclose ₹ 2.10 crore as contingent liability
option_d: No provision — the entire amount is disputed and can only be recognised after the appeal is decided
explanation_html:
The two components require different treatment:

₹ 0.66 crore (not being appealed): By not appealing against this portion, the company has effectively accepted this as a definite obligation. This represents a present obligation with probable outflow → Provision of ₹ 0.66 crore must be created in the accounts.

₹ 2.76 crore paid under protest: The amount paid under protest (the entire ₹ 2.76 crore) should be shown as Loans & Advances (a receivable/deposit, pending final outcome of appeal).

₹ 2.10 crore (being appealed): The outcome is uncertain — this is a contingent liability to be disclosed in the notes as per AS 29, not provided for (since the appeal makes the outflow only possible, not probable at this stage).

question_html: Under AS 15, Termination Benefits should be recognised as a liability and an expense when:
option_a: The employee submits a resignation or requests voluntary retirement
option_b: Management orally communicates its intent to terminate employees
option_c: The enterprise has a detailed formal plan for termination which is duly approved AND a reliable estimate of the obligation can be made
option_d: A provision for retrenchment is created in the annual budget of the enterprise
explanation_html:
Under AS 15, Termination Benefits are recognised as a liability and an expense only when the enterprise has:
(i) A detailed formal plan for the termination which is duly approved, and
(ii) A reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation.

Merely having management's oral communication or budgeting for termination does not meet the recognition criteria. AS 15 requires more certainty — for example, employees must have signed up for the termination scheme before recognition is appropriate. Where there is uncertainty about the number of employees who will accept a voluntary redundancy offer, a contingent liability exists and must be disclosed as per AS 29.

question_html: Accounting Standard 10, Property, Plant and Equipment is applicable to:
option_a: Biological Assets (other than Bearer Plants) related to agricultural activity
option_b: Wasting Assets including Mineral rights, Expenditure on the exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources
explanation_html:
AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment) does NOT apply to certain categories of assets — these are specifically excluded from its scope:

  • Biological assets (other than bearer plants) related to agricultural activity — excluded from AS 10 scope.
  • Wasting assets including mineral rights, exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources — excluded.
  • Inventories — covered by AS 2, not AS 10.

AS 10 IS applicable to:

  • Bearer Plants (except produce growing on bearer plants). A bearer plant is a living plant used in the production or supply of agricultural produce, expected to bear produce for more than one period (e.g., tea bushes, grape vines, rubber trees). Bearer plants are treated as PPE under AS 10, though the produce on them is accounted for separately under AS on Agriculture.

Therefore, AS 10 applies to Bearer Plants (except produce on Bearer Plants) — option (d).

question_html: Arka Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹ 3,000 lakhs (SLM, 10% p.a., 10 years). At end of Year 4, it is revalued to ₹ 2,700 lakhs. What is the carrying amount at the end of Year 6?
explanation_html:
Step 1: Book value at end of Year 4 = ₹3,000 – (₹3,000 × 10% × 4) = ₹3,000 – ₹1,200 = ₹1,800 lakhs.
Revaluation to ₹2,700 lakhs; Revaluation surplus = ₹900 lakhs.

Step 2: Remaining useful life = 10 – 4 = 6 years.
Revised annual depreciation = ₹2,700 ÷ 6 = ₹450 lakhs p.a.

Step 3: Carrying amount at end of Year 5 = ₹2,700 – ₹450 = ₹2,250 lakhs.
Carrying amount at end of Year 6 = ₹2,250 – ₹450 = ₹1,800 lakhs.

question_html: In the Surrender of Shares method of internal reconstruction, what happens to the surrendered shares that are NOT re-issued to debenture holders or creditors?

2. Shareholders surrender some of their shares to the company

question_html: P Ltd. acquires 80% of S Ltd. on 31st March 20X1 by paying ₹ 1,000. S Ltd.'s net worth on that date = ₹ 1,000 (Share Capital ₹ 700, Reserves ₹ 300). What is the Goodwill/(Capital Reserve) on consolidation?
option_b: Capital Reserve ₹ 200 (P Ltd. paid less than net worth)
option_c: Goodwill ₹ 200 (cost ₹1,000 exceeds P Ltd.'s 80% share of net worth ₹800)
option_d: Nil — no goodwill or capital reserve arises
explanation_html:
Under AS 21, Goodwill = Cost of Investment – Parent's share in equity of subsidiary at date of investment.

Net worth of S Ltd. = ₹700 + ₹300 = ₹1,000.
P Ltd.'s share (80%) = 80% × ₹1,000 = ₹800.
Cost of Investment = ₹1,000.
Goodwill = ₹1,000 – ₹800 = ₹200.

Key insight: Even though total net worth equals the cost paid, P Ltd. acquired only 80% — so only 80% of the net worth is the "intrinsic value" being acquired. The excess paid (₹200) over P Ltd.'s proportionate share represents goodwill. The remaining 20% (₹200) belongs to Minority Interest.

question_html: As per the Debt-Equity Ratio Test under the Companies Act, 2013, what is the maximum debt that can be owed by a company after the buy-back?

explanation_html:
The Debt-Equity Ratio Test under Section 68(2)(e) states: The ratio of the debt owed by the company (both secured and unsecured) after such buy-back should NOT be more than TWICE the total of its paid-up capital and its free reserves.

In ratio form: Debt : Equity (post buy-back) ≤ 2:1

Note: Debt includes both long-term and short-term debt. Free reserves include securities premium for this purpose. Capital Redemption Reserve (created on buy-back) is NOT a free reserve and is excluded from this computation. The Central Government may prescribe a higher ratio for specific classes of companies.

question_html: A partnership firm's governing statute does not require compliance with Accounting Standards. When the auditor of such a firm discharges attest functions, the mandatory status of Accounting Standards implies that the auditor must:
option_a: Refuse to sign the audit report if any deviation from Accounting Standards exists

option_c: Prepare revised financial statements in compliance with AS before signing the report
option_d: Ignore the Accounting Standards entirely since the statute does not mandate compliance
explanation_html: Where the statute governing the enterprise does not require compliance with Accounting Standards (e.g., a partnership firm), the mandatory status of an AS implies that members of ICAI, in discharging their attest functions, are required to examine whether financial statements are prepared in compliance with applicable AS. In the event of any deviation, they have the duty to make adequate disclosures in their reports so that users are aware. The responsibility for preparing financial statements and making adequate disclosure rests with management. The auditor's responsibility is to form his opinion and report on such financial statements. The auditor cannot refuse to sign the report merely on grounds of AS deviation, nor is it his duty to revise the financial statements.

question_html: As per AS 17, the 75% Overall Test requires that:
option_a: At least 75% of total enterprise assets must be covered by reportable segments
option_b: At least 75% of total enterprise profit must be covered by reportable segments
option_c: At least 75% of total enterprise revenue (external sales only) must be attributable to reportable segments; additional segments are added if needed even if they do not meet the 10% tests
option_d: At least 75% of total enterprise revenue (external and internal) must be attributable to reportable segments after applying the 10% tests
explanation_html: The 75% Overall Test under AS 17 states: if total external revenue attributable to reportable segments constitutes less than 75% of the total enterprise revenue (external), additional segments must be identified as reportable segments — even if they do not meet the 10% thresholds — until at least 75% of total enterprise revenue is included in reportable segments. Key points: (i) The 75% test uses external revenue only, not inter-segment. (ii) The 10% revenue test uses both external and internal revenue. This distinction is frequently tested. The purpose of the 75% test is to ensure sufficient coverage of the enterprise in segment disclosures.

question_html: As per AS 29, a Restructuring Provision should include:
option_a: Retraining costs of continuing staff and marketing costs for new product lines
option_b: Investment in new distribution networks after restructuring
option_c: Only the direct expenditures necessarily entailed by the restructuring and not associated with ongoing activities of the enterprise
option_d: All costs expected to be incurred from the date the restructuring plan is announced
explanation_html:
As per AS 29, a restructuring provision should include only the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring, which are those that are both:
(a) Necessarily entailed by the restructuring; and
(b) Not associated with the ongoing activities of the enterprise.

A restructuring provision does NOT include:
• Retraining or relocating continuing staff
• Marketing costs
• Investment in new systems and distribution networks

These relate to the future conduct of the business and are not present obligations for restructuring at the balance sheet date. Also, no provision can be made for a sale of an operation until there is a binding sale agreement. Future operating losses up to the date of restructuring are also excluded from the provision.

explanation_html:

question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in the separate financial statement of G Ltd. as on 31.3.2024?
explanation_html:
In the separate financial statements of G Ltd., investment in Build Ltd. (an associate) is accounted under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments) — at cost less any dividend received that constitutes a return of investment (reduction in cost).

Investment cost on 1.7.2023 = ₹14,00,000.

Build Ltd. paid dividend of ₹1,50,000 on 15.7.2023 for the year ending 31.3.2023. G Ltd.'s share = 35% × ₹1,50,000 = ₹52,500.

This dividend relates to pre-acquisition profits (the year ending 31.3.2023 — before G Ltd. acquired the shares on 1.7.2023). Under AS 13, dividend received out of pre-acquisition profits reduces the cost of investment.

Carrying amount = ₹14,00,000 − ₹52,500 = ₹13,47,500.

Note: Equity method (with share of post-acquisition profit) applies only in Consolidated Financial Statements, not in separate FS.

question_html: The Framework identifies how many broad groups of users of financial statements?
explanation_html: As per the Framework, there are seven broad groups of users of financial statements: Investors, Employees, Lenders, Suppliers and other trade creditors, Customers, Governments and their agencies, and Public. All these groups use financial statements to satisfy some of their information needs for making economic decisions.

question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in Separate Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2024?
explanation_html:
In separate financial statements, investment in an associate is accounted under AS 13 (Accounting for Investments) — at cost less dividend received that is a return of investment (pre-acquisition dividend).

Investment cost = ₹5,00,000 on 01.07.2023.

Moon Ltd. declared dividend of ₹80,000 for FY 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. Sun Ltd.'s share = 40% × ₹80,000 = ₹32,000.

This dividend is for the year ending 31.3.2023 — before Sun acquired shares on 01.07.2023. It relates to pre-acquisition profits → reduces cost of investment.

Carrying amount in separate FS = ₹5,00,000 − ₹32,000 = ₹4,68,000.

Note: The dividend declared for FY 2023-24 (₹90,000) was declared on 15.09.2024 — after the balance sheet date of 31.03.2024. It does not affect the 31.3.2024 carrying value.

question_html: Rau Ltd. purchased a plant for US$ 1,00,000 on 1st February 20X1, payable after 3 months. The company entered into a forward contract @ ₹ 49.15 per dollar. Spot rate on 1st Feb = ₹ 48.85. The contract is NOT for trading/speculation. How should the premium be recognised?
option_a: Loss of ₹ 30,000 recognised entirely in the year ended 31st March 20X1
option_b: Loss of ₹ 30,000 recognised entirely in the year following 31st March 20X1
option_c: Loss amortised over 3 months: ₹ 20,000 recognised in FY ended 31st March 20X1; ₹ 10,000 in the following year
option_d: Premium is ignored since the contract is not for speculation
explanation_html:
For a forward exchange contract not intended for trading or speculation (i.e., a hedging contract), AS 11 requires:

Premium/Discount: The difference between forward rate (₹49.15) and spot rate (₹48.85) = ₹0.30 per dollar. Total premium (loss) = ₹0.30 × 1,00,000 = ₹30,000. This should be amortised as expense over the life of the contract (3 months).

Contract period = 3 months (1st Feb to 30th Apr 20X1). Of these, 2 months fall in FY 20X1 (Feb and March) and 1 month in FY 20X2.

FY 20X1: (₹30,000 ÷ 3) × 2 = ₹20,000
FY 20X2: (₹30,000 ÷ 3) × 1 = ₹10,000

question_html: A piece of information is said to be 'material' if:
option_a: It relates to a large monetary amount in the financial statements
option_b: Its misstatement (omission or erroneous statement) can influence economic decisions of a user taken on the basis of financial information
option_c: It is mandatorily required to be disclosed under law
option_d: It appears in the Balance Sheet rather than the Profit and Loss Account
explanation_html: As per the Framework, a piece of information is said to be material if its misstatement (i.e., omission or erroneous statement) can influence economic decisions of a user taken on the basis of the financial information. Materiality depends on the size AND nature of the item or error, judged in the specific circumstances of its misstatement. Importantly, materiality provides a threshold or cut-off point rather than being a primary qualitative characteristic which the information must have if it is to be useful.

question_html: How should the interest on income tax refunds should be disclosed in the Cash Flows Statement:
explanation_html:
As per AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements), interest received is generally classified under Investing Activities for non-financial enterprises.

Interest on income tax refund is essentially interest income received from the government — it is classified under Cash flows from Investing Activities since it represents a return on amounts deposited with tax authorities (analogous to interest on deposits/investments).

question_html: As per AS 15, the seven components of Defined Benefit Costs to be recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss include all of the following EXCEPT:
option_b: Expected return on plan assets and actuarial gains and losses
option_d: Past service cost and effect of any curtailments or settlements
explanation_html:
AS 15 identifies seven components of defined benefit costs recognised in P&L:
(a) Current service cost
(b) Interest cost
(c) Expected return on plan assets (and reimbursement rights)
(d) Actuarial gains and losses (recognised immediately)
(e) Past service cost
(f) Effect of curtailments or settlements
(g) Extent to which the negative net defined benefit liability exceeds the economic benefit available

Employee's own contribution to the plan is NOT a component of the employer's defined benefit cost — it reduces the employer's obligation or plan assets but is not an employer's expense in P&L. The standard prescribes accounting in the books of the employer, and employee contributions reduce the employer's net defined benefit liability.

question_html: All of the following costs are excluded while computing value of inventories except?
option_b: Allocated fixed production overheads based on normal capacity.
option_d: Storage costs (which is necessary part of the production process)
explanation_html:
As per AS 2 (Valuation of Inventories), costs excluded from inventory include: selling and distribution costs, abnormal wastage, storage costs (unless necessary in production process), and administrative overheads unrelated to current location/condition.

Allocated fixed production overheads based on normal capacity are included in inventory cost — they are part of conversion costs. The phrase "based on normal capacity" is key: overhead per unit is calculated at normal, not actual, capacity utilisation.

question_html: As per AS 3, the Cash Flow Statement is mandatory for which of the following companies under the Companies Act, 2013?

option_d: All companies except those with paid-up share capital below ₹ 50 lakhs
explanation_html: Under Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013, the financial statements with respect to One Person Company, Small Company, Dormant Company, and private company (if such a private company is a start-up) may not include the Cash Flow Statement. The start-up private company exemption was added via Notification dated 13th June, 2017 under Section 462 of the Companies Act, 2013. All other companies are mandatorily required to prepare Cash Flow Statements. For non-corporate entities, AS 3 is mandatory only for Non-SMCs (and Level I entities for non-corporates); it is only encouraged for others.

question_html: What is the maximum number of shares that can be bought back according to the Resources Test?
explanation_html:
The Resources Test limits buy-back to 25% of total paid-up capital and free reserves.

Free Reserves = Revenue Reserve + Securities Premium + Profit & Loss Account = ₹ 23,50,000 + ₹ 2,50,000 + ₹ 2,00,000 = ₹ 28,00,000. (Infrastructure Development Reserve is a statutory reserve — not freely available.)

Total paid-up capital and free reserves = ₹ 17,00,000 + ₹ 28,00,000 = ₹ 45,00,000

Maximum buy-back amount = 25% × ₹ 45,00,000 = ₹ 11,25,000

Maximum shares = ₹ 11,25,000 ÷ ₹ 30 (buy-back price) = 37,500 shares

You are required to state whether Mr. Abhishek is eligible to inspect the books of accounts of Ganesh Company Limited?
option_a: Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company limited only on authorization of the public financial institution on whose behalf he has been so appointed in the board of the Ganesh Company Ltd.
option_b: No. Mr. Abhishek being a nominee director can only inspect the books of accounts of Ganesh Company Ltd and not its subsidiary company.
option_c: Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company limited only on authorization by way of resolution of the board of directors.
option_d: Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company limited only on authorization by way of resolution of the members holding not less than 25% of the paid-up share capital of the company.
explanation_html:
The correct answer is (C): Yes, Mr. Abhishek can inspect the books of accounts of Shankar Company limited only on authorization by way of resolution of the board of directors..

question_html: AB Ltd. has received a legal notice from a customer claiming damages of ₹ 5,00,000. The company's lawyers advise that it is NOT probable yet that resources will be required to settle the claim. According to AS 29, the correct accounting treatment is:
option_a: Create a provision of ₹ 5,00,000 since the amount is known
option_b: Disclose as a contingent liability in the notes to financial statements
option_c: No provision, no disclosure since the likelihood is not probable
explanation_html:
When an outflow of resources is not probable (i.e., it is possible but not more likely than not), AS 29 requires disclosure as a contingent liability in the notes to the financial statements — as long as the possibility of outflow is not remote.

The three-level decision framework under AS 29:
1. Probable outflow → Recognise a provision
2. Possible outflow (not probable) → Disclose as contingent liability
3. Remote outflow → Neither provision nor disclosure

In AB Ltd.'s case, since lawyers advise the claim is 'not probable yet' (but the possibility is not stated as remote), the appropriate treatment is disclosure as a contingent liability. Option (c) would be correct only if the possibility of outflow were remote.

question_html: As per the requirements of AS 3, 'Cash Flow Statements', how the amount for purchase of machinery should be presented:
option_a: ₹ 10 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Investing Activities' and ₹ 30,000 will simply be booked in profit and loss with no presentation if Cash Flow Statement.
option_b: ₹ 10.30 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Investing Activities' as entire amount is spend on purchase of machinery.
option_c: ₹ 10 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Investing Activities' and ₹ 30,000 as 'Cash flows from Financing Activities'.
option_d: ₹ 10.30 lakhs as 'Cash flows from Financing Activities' as the machinery has been purchased on finance.
explanation_html:
As per AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements):

  • The cost of the machinery (₹10 lakhs) represents an acquisition of PPE — classified as Investing Activities (outflow).
  • The interest component (₹30,000) embedded in the deferred payment instalments represents a financing cost — classified as Financing Activities (outflow).

These two components are separated and presented in their respective categories. The principal of the deferred payment (₹6 lakhs) is part of the ₹10 lakhs asset cost shown as investing, while the interest (₹30,000) is financing.

question_html: Under AS 14 (Purchase Method), how are Statutory Reserves of the transferor company (e.g., Investment Allowance Reserve, Export Profit Reserve) treated in the books of the transferee company?
option_a: They are merged with the transferee's General Reserve
option_b: They are completely written off since purchase amalgamation doesn't preserve identity of reserves
option_c: They retain their identity — credited to Statutory Reserve; debit to 'Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve' (shown as a negative balance in Reserves and Surplus)
option_d: They are treated as capital reserve of the transferee company
explanation_html:
In a purchase amalgamation, normally the identity of reserves of the transferor is NOT preserved. However, AS 14 makes an exception for statutory reserves (reserves maintained under the requirements of law, e.g., Investment Allowance Reserve, Export Profit Reserve under Income Tax Act).

These must retain their identity. The journal entry is:
Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve A/c Dr. (negative reserve — debit balance shown as deduction)
   To Statutory Reserve Cr.

The Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve is shown as a separate negative line item under Reserves and Surplus — it cannot be set off against the Statutory Reserve. Once the statutory requirement period ends, both are reversed.

As seen in Illustration 8 (X Ltd.): Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve (300) is shown as a negative ₹300 thousands against Investment Allowance Reserve ₹100 thousands.

question_html: What is the key difference between Internal Reconstruction and External Reconstruction?
option_a: Internal reconstruction requires approval from SEBI; external reconstruction does not
option_b: In internal reconstruction, the existing company is NOT liquidated but its capital/debt structure is changed. In external reconstruction, the existing company is liquidated and a new company is formed with substantially the same shareholders
option_c: Internal reconstruction always involves creation of new shares; external reconstruction never does
option_d: Internal reconstruction is governed by AS 14; external reconstruction is governed by Section 66
explanation_html:
The fundamental distinction:

Internal Reconstruction: The existing company is NOT liquidated. Instead, its capital and debt structure is changed to bring it back to normalcy. The company continues its existence with a reorganized balance sheet. Governed by Sections 61 and 66 of the Companies Act, 2013. Requires Court/Tribunal confirmation.

External Reconstruction: The existing company IS liquidated to form a new company. The existing shareholders become shareholders of the new company. The business of the old company is transferred to the new company. Governed by Section 232 of the Companies Act, 2013. AS 14 classifies this as "Amalgamation in the nature of merger."

External reconstruction requires less time and court interference; internal reconstruction involves more legal procedures.

question_html: A government company shall not raise deposits exceeding____of its paid–up share capital, free reserves and securities premium.

question_html: Zenith Pharmaceuticals Ltd. paid a penalty of ₹ 75,000 for breach of environmental regulations during the year. The company's total revenue was ₹ 850 crore. The accountant proposes to club this penalty with 'Legal and Professional Charges' in the financial statements since it is insignificant in amount. As per Accounting Standards, this treatment is:
option_a: Correct, because ₹ 75,000 is immaterial relative to ₹ 850 crore revenue and can be clubbed
option_b: Incorrect, because the penalty is a material item due to the information it conveys and must be disclosed separately
option_c: Correct, because materiality is always determined solely by the absolute size of the amount
option_d: Incorrect, because all expenses must always be disclosed as separate line items regardless of materiality
explanation_html: This question tests a critical concept — materiality is NOT necessarily a function of size. Even though ₹ 75,000 appears insignificant compared to ₹ 850 crore revenue, it is a material item because of the information it conveys — namely, that the company has breached a law. This is specifically illustrated in the ICAI material with the example of a penalty of ₹ 50,000 paid for breach of law. It is not appropriate to club penalties paid with legal charges. If an item is material (based on its information content), it should be shown separately. Option (a) incorrectly assumes materiality is only size-based. Option (d) is too absolute and incorrect.

question_html: As per the Companies Act, 2013, every buy-back must be completed within what time frame from the date of passing the special resolution (or board resolution)?
explanation_html:
As per the Companies Act, 2013, every buy-back shall be completed within twelve months (1 year) from the date of passing the special resolution, or the resolution passed by the Board of Directors.

Additional time-related provisions:
• No offer of buy-back shall be made within a period of one year from the date of closure of a previous buy-back offer (minimum gap between two buy-backs).
• After completion of buy-back, the company shall not make further issue of same kind of shares within 6 months (except bonus issue, conversion of warrants/debentures/preference shares, sweat equity, stock options).
• Return must be filed with ROC (and SEBI for listed companies) within 30 days of completion of buy-back.
